notes.title: Start here: eShopOnWeb and its upskill curriculum
notes.body:
This repo holds Microsoft's **eShopOnWeb**, an official reference e-commerce app (catalog, basket, checkout, orders, admin) built on .NET 8 with Clean Architecture. The `eShopOnWeb/fabledocs/` folder is a curriculum built on it. Every quiz in this pack comes from the **architecture and patterns** track, mostly from two files.

Suggested reading order:

1. `fabledocs/README.md`: the seven-sentence identity of the app and the recommended paths.
2. `fabledocs/00-fast-track.md` if you are new to the code.
3. `03-architecture-and-patterns/01-boundaries-and-layers.md`: the four projects and which may depend on which.
4. `03-architecture-and-patterns/02-data-model-and-persistence.md`: the two databases, mapping decisions, transaction boundaries, migrations.
5. `03-architecture-and-patterns/05-pattern-catalog.md`: sixteen patterns, each with a real example, failure modes and a drill.

The pattern catalog uses one shape per entry: problem, general shape, real example, why it works here, failure modes, interview angle, drill. Do each drill with the linked file open; the quizzes are close to them.

excerpts.quote: It is a deliberately **monolithic** e-commerce store — catalog, basket, checkout, orders, admin — built on .NET 8
Sixteen patterns this repo actually uses, each with the problem it solves, real anchors, failure modes, and an interview angle.

readMore.why: Learning tracks and recommended paths through the curriculum.
The layer rules the patterns rely on.

notes.title: Clean Architecture in four projects
notes.body:
eShopOnWeb splits its code so that the business rules do not depend on frameworks or the database:

- **ApplicationCore**: entities (Basket, Order, CatalogItem), domain services and *interfaces* such as the repository and email sender. No EF Core, no ASP.NET.
- **Infrastructure**: the EF Core data layer and other implementations of those interfaces.
- **Web**, **PublicApi**, **BlazorAdmin**: three user-facing surfaces (a Razor Pages store, a minimal-API backend, an admin panel).

The rule is that dependencies point **inward**: outer projects know about the core, never the other way round. The core declares what it needs as an interface; Infrastructure provides it; dependency injection connects the two at startup.

As you read the pattern catalog, watch for the same move repeated: put the rule or contract in the core, keep frameworks at the edge. Patterns 1 (Clean Architecture), 2 (Repository) and 7 (Composition Root) are three views of the same idea. Pattern 4 (Aggregate) is about rules inside the core itself.

excerpts.quote: It demonstrates **Clean Architecture**: a dependency-free domain project (`ApplicationCore`), an EF Core data layer (`Infrastructure`), and three UI surfaces
**General shape:** a dependency-free core defines interfaces; outer layers implement them; the dependency arrow points inward.

notes.title: EF Core: what is saved together, and what a migration must handle
notes.body:
The data-model chapter teaches two habits for working with a database through EF Core.

**Know your unit of consistency.** EF Core tracks changes in a `DbContext` and writes them when you call `SaveChanges`. Everything in one `SaveChanges` is saved atomically. The chapter lists places in the app that call save more than once in a row, and asks what a crash in between would leave behind.

**Read every migration.** A migration is the generated code that changes the database schema to match your model. Some changes are easy (adding a nullable column); others touch existing rows (making a column required, renaming, dropping). The chapter gives a six-step playbook and a "blast radius" ranking, and walks through one real migration as a case study.

The chapter's mapping table is also worth learning: each row names a mapping decision, the file and lines that make it, why, and the interview vocabulary for it.

excerpts.quote: The unit of consistency in EF is `SaveChanges` — everything tracked in a context is saved atomically.
adding a nullable column is low-risk (additive); making a column non-null, renaming, or dropping is high-risk

notes.title: What is wrong with OrderWithItemsByIdSpec
notes.body:
The key is right: it has no buyer filter, so a user can load another user's order by id. A **specification** is a named, reusable query. This one has a single `Where`: `order.Id == orderId`. Nothing checks that the order belongs to the person asking. Any logged-in user who guesses or changes an order id could load someone else's order. That is an IDOR (insecure direct object reference). The pattern catalog lists exactly this as a failure mode: a spec missing a security filter, "literally a spec that forgot a `Where`". The drill asks you to add the predicate (on the buyer id).

Why the others are wrong:
- "No paging, so it times out": it loads one order; paging is for lists.
- "Over-fetches the whole catalog graph": the includes stop at the order's items and their ordered-item snapshot.
- "Not reusable, id hard-coded": the id is a constructor parameter, so the spec works for any order.

excerpts.quote: Query .Where(order => order.Id == orderId) .Include(o => o.OrderItems) .ThenInclude(i => i.ItemOrdered);
a spec missing a security filter (the Flow 7 IDOR is literally a spec that forgot a `Where`).

notes.title: The classic DI lifetime bug
notes.body:
The key is right: a singleton capturing a scoped `DbContext`, called a **captive dependency**. A singleton is created once for the whole app. A `DbContext` is registered as scoped: one per web request. If a singleton receives a `DbContext` in its constructor, it keeps that one context forever, shared by every request and thread, long after the request it belonged to ended. The pattern catalog names it in Pattern 7's failure modes and repeats it in the interview angle.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Constructor injection instead of a service locator": constructor injection is the recommended approach; the service-locator style is the anti-pattern.
- "Repositories as transient instead of scoped": not the bug named; the repo registers them scoped.
- "Open-generic registration of the repository": the catalog praises that one-line registration in "why it works here".

excerpts.quote: **Failure modes:** wrong lifetime (a singleton capturing a scoped DbContext — a classic bug)
the DbContext-in-a-singleton captive-dependency trap.
wires every entity's repository in one line.

notes.title: The REPR failure mode for a new write endpoint
notes.body:
The key is right: nothing forces a new endpoint to declare the `ADMINISTRATORS` requirement. With one class per endpoint (REPR: Request-Endpoint-Response), each class declares its own route **and its own authorization**. That keeps everything about an endpoint in one place. But there is no shared base class or controller attribute that applies to all of them, so a developer who forgets the role check on a new write endpoint ships an endpoint anyone can call. The catalog's failure mode says "auth attribute forgotten on a new endpoint (nothing forces it)", and the drill asks you to check every write endpoint.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Loses access to DI": endpoints get their services injected like anything else.
- "Cannot share DTOs": DTOs are ordinary classes; nothing stops sharing.
- "Registered twice": `AddEndpoints()` and `MapEndpoints()` are the two steps of one registration, not duplicates.

excerpts.quote: each endpoint implements `IEndpoint<...>`, declares its own route + auth, and is auto-registered.
auth attribute forgotten on a new endpoint (nothing forces it).
cohesion and discoverability vs. more files and no enforced base behavior.

notes.title: Why there is a repository for Basket but not BasketItem
notes.body:
The key is right: the generic repository requires its type to implement `IAggregateRoot`, and `BasketItem` does not. `EfRepository` is declared with the constraint `where T : class, IAggregateRoot`. The compiler will only let you create a repository for a type that implements that marker interface. `Basket` does; `BasketItem` does not. The point is an **aggregate boundary**: a basket item only makes sense inside its basket, so you should always load and change it through the basket. The catalog: you can't accidentally load a `BasketItem` independent of its `Basket`.

Why the others are wrong:
- "BasketItem is a value object without an Id": it is an entity with its own table (BasketItems); it is just not a root.
- "Repositories are registered by hand for Basket and Order": registration is one open-generic line for every type.
- "No DbSet of its own": the reason is the type constraint, not EF.

excerpts.quote: where T : class, IAggregateRoot
means only aggregate roots get repositories — you can't accidentally load a `BasketItem` independent of its `Basket`.
open-generic registration

notes.title: Why the guard clauses live inside CatalogItem
notes.body:
The key is right: so an invalid `CatalogItem` cannot exist, whoever constructs it. A **guard clause** is a check at the top of a method that throws if an argument is bad (`Guard.Against.X(...)`). If the checks only lived in a controller, any other code path (a different endpoint, a test, a seed script) could build a broken item. Putting them in the entity's own methods means the rule is enforced at the entity boundary, every time. The catalog names "guarding in the controller but not the domain" as a failure mode.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Minimal API endpoints may not throw": endpoints can throw; this is about where the rule lives.
- "Checked at compile time": guard clauses run when the code runs; they throw exceptions.
- "Friendlier, localised messages": the catalog says guards are distinct from user-facing model validation, and warns that generic guard exceptions are hard for the UI to tell apart.

excerpts.quote: **Why it works here:** invariants are enforced at the entity boundary, so an invalid `CatalogItem` can't exist.
guarding in the controller but not the domain (so tests bypass it)
guard clauses at boundaries + domain-level invariants, distinct from user-facing model validation.

notes.title: How catalog caching is added without touching callers
notes.body:
The key is right: a cached wrapper implements the same interface, and DI registers it instead. This is the **decorator** pattern. `CachedCatalogViewModelService` implements `ICatalogViewModelService` and holds the real `CatalogViewModelService` inside. It answers from the cache when it can and calls the real service otherwise. In `ConfigureWebServices.cs`, the interface is mapped to the cached class, so every caller that asks for `ICatalogViewModelService` gets the cached one without knowing. Removing caching is one DI line.

Why the others are wrong:
- "EF Core's second-level cache": no such thing is switched on; the caching is in the Web project's own class.
- "Response-caching middleware": the catalog's example is a service-level wrapper, not HTTP response caching.
- "Inherits from a caching base class": a decorator *wraps* the real class through the shared interface; it does not inherit from it.

excerpts.quote: ICatalogViewModelService, CachedCatalogViewModelService>();
**General shape:** a class implements the same interface, holds an instance of the real one, and adds behavior around delegated calls.
callers depend on `ICatalogViewModelService` and never know caching exists; you could remove the decorator by changing one DI line.

notes.title: Why FixShipToAddress needs a default value
notes.body:
The key is right: the NOT NULL change would fail on rows that still hold nulls. Making a column `NOT NULL` tells the database "no row may be empty here". If existing rows already hold null in that column, the database refuses the change, because those rows would break the new rule straight away. The migration's `defaultValue: ""` fills those rows with an empty string, so the constraint can be applied. The chapter calls this the migration author handling **existing rows**, and notes the migration also has a real `Down`, so it can be reversed.

Why the others are wrong:
- "EF would delete the null rows": migrations do not delete data to make a constraint fit.
- "It would succeed and nulls would stay": a NOT NULL column cannot hold nulls.
- "Down would run automatically": `Down` only runs when you roll back on purpose.

excerpts.quote: That default-value choice is the migration author handling **existing rows** that had nulls; without it, the `ALTER` would fail on existing null data.
without the default, `ALTER COLUMN ... NOT NULL` fails on rows where the value is null; the default backfills those rows so the constraint can be applied.

notes.title: Why an order item copies the product name and picture
notes.body:
The key is right: to preserve what was bought, even if the catalog item later changes. An order is a historical record. If an order line only pointed at the live catalog item, renaming the product or changing its picture would quietly change every past order that contains it. Copying the name and picture into `CatalogItemOrdered` at purchase time keeps the order exactly as it was. The chapter's mapping table calls it a snapshot embedded in OrderItems, "denormalization for history".

Why the others are wrong:
- "EF cannot map a foreign key there": EF maps foreign keys easily; this is a modeling choice.
- "Owned types are faster than a join": speed is not the reason given.
- "So past orders can be corrected by editing the catalog item": the opposite; the copy exists so catalog edits do *not* change past orders.

excerpts.quote: | `CatalogItemOrdered` as owned type | [OrderItemConfiguration.cs:11-18](../../src/Infrastructure/Data/Config/OrderItemConfiguration.cs#L11-L18) | Snapshot embedded in OrderItems | denormalization for history |
a snapshot value object.

notes.title: What Basket.AddItem does with an item already in the basket
notes.body:
The key is right: the existing line's quantity grows, and the rule is safe because `AddItem` is the only thing that can change the private item list. `AddItem` first checks `Items.Any(i => i.CatalogItemId == catalogItemId)`. If there is no line for that product, it adds one. If there is, it finds it and calls `AddQuantity`. The list itself is a private `_items` field; the public `Items` property is `_items.AsReadOnly()`. So no other code can add a second line behind the basket's back. The rule "one line per catalog item" lives in one place.

Why the others are wrong:
- "BasketService checks for a duplicate first": the check is inside the `Basket` entity itself.
- "A unique index rejects the duplicate": no such index is involved; the code never tries to add a duplicate.
- "A second line is added, and the UI merges them": `AddItem` updates the existing line instead.

excerpts.quote: if (!Items.Any(i => i.CatalogItemId == catalogItemId)) { _items.Add(new BasketItem(catalogItemId, quantity, unitPrice)); return; } var existingItem = Items.First(i => i.CatalogItemId == catalogItemId); existingItem.AddQuantity(quantity);
Items => _items.AsReadOnly();
the invariant "one line per catalog item" is enforced in one place

notes.title: What HiLo id generation buys
notes.body:
The key is right: ids are assigned on the client from reserved blocks, so inserts can be batched. With a normal identity column, the database picks each new id at insert time, and EF must wait for it before it knows the row's id. With **HiLo**, EF reserves a block of numbers from a database sequence once, then hands out ids from that block itself, before inserting. Since every new row already has its id, EF can send many inserts together with fewer round trips. The chapter's table says exactly that.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Ids hidden from the public API": HiLo ids are ordinary numbers; nothing hides them.
- "Reuses ids freed by deleted rows": the sequence moves forward; old ids are not reused.
- "Globally unique GUIDs": HiLo produces integers from a sequence, not GUIDs.

excerpts.quote: | **HiLo** id generation | [CatalogItemConfiguration.cs:13-15](../../src/Infrastructure/Data/Config/CatalogItemConfiguration.cs#L13-L15) | Assign ids client-side, batch inserts, fewer round-trips | id strategy |

notes.title: Why the PublicApi returns a DTO instead of the entity
notes.body:
The key is right: contract stability and protection against over-posting. A **DTO** (data transfer object) is a class shaped for the API, separate from the database entity. If the API returned `CatalogItem` directly, every change to the entity would change what clients receive, and any field you add would leak out. On input, binding straight to an entity lets a client set fields you never meant them to (**over-posting**). With a DTO, the API decides its own shape: for example, it renames `CatalogBrand.Brand` to `Name` without touching the entity. The catalog's interview answer lists contract stability, over-posting protection and avoiding accidental data leaks.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Minimal API binding is limited to DTOs": binding works with any class.
- "AutoMapper refuses EF entities": AutoMapper maps entities to DTOs here, which is its normal job.
- "System.Text.Json cannot serialise entities": it can; the catalog's reasons are about design, not ability.

excerpts.quote: **Interview angle:** "Why not return your entities from the API?" → contract stability, over-posting protection, avoiding accidental data leaks.
the API renames `CatalogBrand.Brand` → `dto.Name`
returning entities directly (couples clients to your DB and can leak fields)

notes.title: What a crash between the two checkout saves leaves
notes.body:
The key is right: an order is created, but its basket lingers. Checkout runs two calls in a row: `CreateOrderAsync` (which saves the new order) and then `DeleteBasketAsync` (which saves the basket deletion). Each has its own `SaveChanges`, and nothing wraps them in one transaction. If the app crashes after the first and before the second, the order is safely stored, but the basket that should have been emptied is still there. The chapter calls this the gap worth raising on the money path.

Why the others are wrong:
- "A deleted basket with no order": the order is created first, so that state cannot happen from this crash.
- "A half-written order": the order is one `SaveChanges`, which EF wraps in an implicit transaction, so it is all or nothing.
- "A clean state; EF joins the saves": the chapter says there is no atomicity across calls unless you open a transaction.

excerpts.quote: await _orderService.CreateOrderAsync(BasketModel.Id, new Address("123 Main St.", "Kent", "OH", "United States", "44240")); await _basketService.DeleteBasketAsync(BasketModel.Id);
A crash between them leaves an order with a lingering basket. There's no explicit `BeginTransaction`.
within a single `SaveChanges`, EF wraps changes in an implicit transaction; *across* calls you get no atomicity unless you open one explicitly.

notes.title: What really keeps ApplicationCore free of EF Core and ASP.NET
notes.body:
The key is right: its project file has no reference to EF Core or ASP.NET. In .NET, code can only use a library that its project references. `ApplicationCore.csproj` simply does not reference EF Core or ASP.NET, so domain code cannot call them: it would not compile. The catalog says the domain "literally cannot depend on them". That is stronger than a convention people must remember. The drill asks you to grep `ApplicationCore` for `using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore` and explain what finding nothing proves.

Why the others are wrong:
- "A code review rule": reviews help, but the catalog names the project reference as the actual mechanism.
- "A Roslyn analyzer": none is mentioned.
- "Internal repository interfaces": Infrastructure, a separate project, implements those interfaces; the catalog never mentions access modifiers as the guard.

excerpts.quote: **Why it works here:** `ApplicationCore.csproj` has no reference to EF Core or ASP.NET, so the domain literally cannot depend on them.
**Drill:** grep `ApplicationCore` for `using Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore`. Report what you find and what it proves.
